body: Latvian licence plates are long and white, with the standard blue European strip on the left.

Latvian bollards have a thin, slightly curved shape with a rectangular front reflector and two circular back reflectors, in either white or orange. The black strip is slightly angled and they often have numbers below the front reflector. These are distinct from Estonian and Lithuanian bollards.
Latvian utility poles often have distinctive poletops with hook-shaped insulators arranged in an alternating left-right-left pattern. This feature is rare in other Baltic countries.
Latvia uses white chevrons with red arrows. This is the same as in Lithuania and Poland, but opposite to Estonia, Russia and Ukraine.
Latvia's blue kilometre markers are positioned parallel to the road, which distinguishes them from those in Estonia and Lithuania.
Latvian warning and speed signs are identifiable by their thick red border which has a thin white outline.
Latvian pedestrian signs are unique in the Baltics for having five stripes. The pedestrian figure also has noticeably long legs.
Latvian bus stop signs are unique in the Baltics because the bus depicted has five windows, whereas Estonia and Lithuania's have four.
Latvia uses A-type guardrails with white or red reflectors, distinguishing it from Estonia (no reflectors) and Lithuania (orange reflectors).
The Latvian language is a Baltic language, similar to Lithuanian. It is distinguished by unique letters like vowels with a macron (Ā, Ē, Ī) and consonants with a small hook (Ģ, Ķ, Ļ, Ņ).
The Latvian word for street is 'iela', which is unique to the language.
Latvian house numbers are often displayed on tall rectangular plates in various colours, a style not common in the other Baltic states.
Latvian architecture commonly features a mix of wood and white brick, often with steep corrugated metal roofs. Pastel-colored stone walls are also prevalent.
Latvian directional signs are blue with white text, and can be identified by their more stylized arrowhead compared to the vertical-backed arrows in Estonia and Lithuania.
The region south of Jelgava is a wide, open landscape with more fields and less forest than typical for Latvia.
Downtown Riga is known for its majestic Art Nouveau architecture, a style unique within the Baltic states.
